name: Ironhaven
description:
Grand Haven called itself Coast Guard City USA for over a century. The U.S. Coast Guard Festival was the town's identity, the annual celebration of its relationship with the military branch that patrolled the Great Lakes. When the federal government's authority over the Great Lakes was formally ceded to the GLM Corporate Maritime Authority in 2169, Grand Haven didn't lose its Coast Guard. It got a new one.

Ironhaven is now the eastern Lake Michigan headquarters of Ringo Systems' Maritime Security Division -- the private fleet that enforces shipping lane compliance, interdicts unauthorized lake traffic, and maintains the corponations' collective control over Great Lakes cargo movement. The old Coast Guard station at the channel mouth has been expanded into a fortified naval installation, and the harbor that once hosted fishing charters and sailboat races now docks patrol cutters equipped with autonomous weapons systems and electronic warfare suites. Ringo employs roughly 40% of the local workforce, which gives them the kind of community integration that doesn't require sovereign territory -- when you employ everyone's family, you don't need legal jurisdiction. You have something better.

The town itself has the paradoxical character of a military company town that is also genuinely pleasant to live in. Ringo pays well, provides healthcare, and maintains the public infrastructure as a recruitment incentive. The streets are clean. The schools work. The pier and boardwalk are maintained to a standard that would make the old Coast Guard Festival committee proud. But the pleasantness has a specific texture -- the texture of a place where everyone knows who signs the checks and adjusts their behavior accordingly. Dissent in Ironhaven doesn't get you arrested. It gets your spouse's contract reviewed, your kid's school placement reconsidered, your maintenance request moved to the bottom of the queue. The soft coercion of a company town is more effective than any checkpoint because it works through the things people love.

sights: Ringo patrol cutters in the channel, matte-grey hulls bristling with sensor arrays and weapons that are always technically 'in maintenance mode'
The expanded naval installation at the channel mouth -- old Coast Guard architecture preserved as a facade over military-grade infrastructure
The boardwalk and pier, immaculately maintained, families and off-duty Ringo personnel mixing in a scene that looks normal until you notice everyone is slightly too careful
The Grand Haven lighthouse, still operational, now integrated into Ringo's coastal surveillance network
Training exercises visible from shore -- drone swarms, fast boats, the choreography of private military capability
sounds: Patrol boat engines in the channel -- diesel rumble mixed with the whine of electric combat systems
The musical fountain on the waterfront, still performing nightly shows, Ringo-sponsored and somehow more unsettling for being beautiful
Radio chatter from the maritime operations center, audible on certain frequencies if you know where to listen
The town's normalcy -- kids playing, shops operating, conversations that carefully avoid certain topics
Storm warnings from the coastal alert system, which double as maritime security broadcasts
smells: Lake Michigan -- cleaner here than the southern reaches, cold and mineral
Marine diesel from the patrol fleet
The boardwalk's food vendors -- fried fish, kettle corn, the smell of a town performing 'small town lakeside' with corporate funding
Gun oil, faint but present near the naval installation
atmosphere.feel: Ironhaven feels safe. That's the first thing visitors notice. Clean streets, functioning services, no visible poverty. The second thing visitors notice, if they're paying attention, is the quality of the safety -- the way it's maintained not by community trust but by the ambient awareness that Ringo is watching, Ringo is providing, and Ringo can stop doing both. It's a gilded cage where the bars are made of healthcare and school quality, and that makes it harder to resent than any wall.

demographics: Approximately 18,000 residents, primarily Tier 2-3 with Ringo officer corps at Tier 4. Demographically homogeneous -- Ringo's recruitment pipeline draws from military families and maritime communities, producing a population that skews white, disciplined, and politically compliant. Small civilian population provides service economy functions.
economy: Ringo Maritime Security Division is the economy. Approximately 40% direct employment, another 30% in Ringo-dependent service businesses. Annual Ringo maritime operations budget for the eastern lake sector: Φ1.2 billion. The remaining civilian economy is tourism and fishing, both of which operate at Ringo's pleasure.
power_structure: Ringo Systems exercises de facto control through economic dependency rather than sovereign charter. The municipal government is elected and functional but understands implicitly that policy decisions affecting Ringo operations will not be implemented. The Ringo base commander, currently Captain Irina Vasek, is the most powerful person in town and holds no elected office.
dangers: Crossing Ringo's interests -- not violently dangerous, but career-endingly, community-excludingly dangerous
The naval installation's weapons systems are live and autonomous -- the 'maintenance mode' designation is a legal fiction
Getting caught in maritime security operations -- Ringo's lake patrols have broad authority and limited accountability
The soft coercion of dependency -- the danger isn't violence, it's the slow erosion of the ability to say no
Storm surge -- the harbor infrastructure is military-grade but the residential areas are not
opportunities: Ringo contracts pay well and provide genuine security -- for those willing to accept the terms
Maritime intelligence -- Ironhaven sees all lake traffic on the eastern shore and someone always wants to know what's moving
The naval installation has technology that doesn't exist on the civilian market
Ringo personnel who develop private doubts about their employer's operations -- a potential source of inside information for anyone patient enough to cultivate trust
story_hooks: Captain Vasek has been quietly diverting Ringo resources to investigate something in the deep lake -- off the books, off the record, and increasingly off her own psychological baseline

A Ringo maritime patrol encounters something on the lake that their systems cannot identify and their training did not prepare them for -- and the after-action report is classified above the base commander's clearance
A former Coast Guard family that has lived in Grand Haven for five generations is being pressured to sell their lakefront property for a Ringo installation expansion -- and they have decided to fight

adjacent_to: Tulip Protocol / Holland (south along the coast)
Muskegon / The Mill (north along the coast)

frequented_by: Ringo Maritime Security personnel, on and off duty
Military families embedded in the company town
Lake traffic operators seeking clearance or avoiding it
The occasional intelligence operative from a competing corponation, posing as a tourist and fooling nobody
